rows.note: Arabic al-insān means a human being or humankind, as Hebrew אנוש and Biblical Aramaic אנש mean a human or mortal person.

rows.explanation: The Hebrew אנוש means “men” in the phrase about the remembrance of them ceasing among men, matching the ayah’s human being.
The Hebrew אֱנוֹשׁ means “mortal man,” matching the ayah’s human being.
The Hebrew אֱנוֹשׁ means “man” in the recurring “What is man?” question, matching the ayah’s generic human.
The Hebrew אֱנוֹשׁ means a human person, matching the ayah’s “human being.”
The Hebrew אֱנוֹשׁ means “man” in “as man seeth,” matching the ayah’s human being.
The Hebrew אֱנוֹשׁ means “man” born of a woman, matching the ayah’s human being.
The Hebrew אֱנוֹשׁ means “man” in the question about human purity, matching the ayah’s human being.
The Hebrew אֱנוֹשׁ means “man” in the question about being justified before God, matching the ayah’s human being.
The Hebrew אֱנוֹשׁ means “man” who does not know wisdom’s price, matching the ayah’s human being.
The Hebrew אֱנוֹשׁ means “man” in the claim that God is greater than man, matching the ayah’s human being.
The Hebrew אֱנוֹשׁ means “man” in “What is man, that thou art mindful of him?”, a recurring human-being formula.
The Hebrew אֱנוֹשׁ means “man” in “let not man prevail,” matching the ayah’s human being.
The Hebrew אֱנוֹשׁ means “men” in the line that nations may know they are but men, matching the ayah’s human being.
The Hebrew אֱנוֹשׁ means “man” whom God turns back to dust, matching the ayah’s human being.
The Hebrew אֱנוֹשׁ means “man” whose days are like grass, matching the ayah’s human being.
The Hebrew אֱנוֹשׁ means “man” whose heart is gladdened by wine, matching the ayah’s human being.
The Hebrew אֱנוֹשׁ means “man” in “What is man, that thou takest knowledge of him?”, a recurring human-being formula.
The Hebrew אֱנוֹשׁ means “a man” in “a man’s pen,” matching the ayah’s human being.
The Hebrew אֱנוֹשׁ means “man” whose heart melts, matching the ayah’s human being.
The Hebrew אֱנוֹשׁ means “men” left on the earth, matching the ayah’s human being.
The Hebrew אֱנוֹשׁ means “a man that shall die,” emphasizing the mortality of the human being.
The Hebrew אֱנוֹשׁ means “men” among whom God showed signs, matching the ayah’s human being.
The Hebrew אָנֻשׁ describes “desperate sorrow,” a shifted sickness or distress sense rather than the ayah’s human noun.
The Hebrew אָנֻשׁ describes the heart as “desperately wicked,” a shifted sickness or incurability sense rather than the ayah’s human noun.
The Hebrew אָנֻשָׁה describes an “incurable” wound, a shifted sickness sense rather than the ayah’s human noun.
The Aramaic אנש means “man” in “there is not a man upon the earth,” matching the ayah’s human being.
The Aramaic אנש means “men” in “the children of men,” matching the ayah’s human being.
The Aramaic אנש means “man” in “a man’s heart,” matching the ayah’s human being.
The Aramaic אנש means “men” in “the sons of men,” matching the ayah’s human being.
The Aramaic אנש means “man” in “one like the Son of man,” matching the ayah’s human being.

rows.note: The ayah’s khusr is a state of loss or ruin, whereas Biblical חסר means to lack, be deficient, or decrease.

rows.explanation: The Hebrew חסר is rendered “the waters were abated,” describing a decrease that evokes loss.
The Hebrew חסר is rendered “the waters decreased continually,” describing reduction rather than the ayah’s human loss.
The Hebrew חסר means “there shall lack five,” expressing a deficiency close to the ayah’s state of loss.
The Hebrew חסר means that the one who gathered little “had no lack,” expressing absence or deficiency.
The Hebrew חסר means “thou hast lacked nothing,” expressing the opposite of being in loss.
The Hebrew חסר means “thou shalt not lack any thing,” expressing deficiency.
The Hebrew מחסור and חסר describe a poor person’s need and what he lacks, a deficiency sense.
The Hebrew מחסור means “want of all things,” a state of deprivation close to the ayah’s loss.
The Hebrew מחסור means “want” in “there is no want of any thing,” expressing lack.
The Hebrew חסר means “lack” in “Do I lack madmen?”, expressing absence.
The Hebrew חסר means the meal and oil will not “fail,” expressing depletion.
The Hebrew חסר means the meal and oil did not “fail,” expressing depletion.
The Hebrew חסר means the people “lacked nothing,” expressing absence or deficiency.
The Hebrew חסר means “I shall not want,” expressing lack, the opposite of the ayah’s loss.
The Hebrew חסר means those who seek the LORD “shall not want any good thing,” expressing lack.
The Hebrew חסר means the wicked person’s belly “shall want,” expressing deficiency.
The Hebrew חסר means the husband “shall have no lack” of spoil, expressing deficiency.
The Hebrew חסר means “let thy head lack no ointment,” expressing absence.
The Hebrew חסר means the drink of the thirsty will “fail,” expressing depletion.
The Hebrew חסר means “we have wanted all things,” a deprivation sense close to the ayah’s loss.
The Hebrew חסר means the people “may want bread and water,” expressing deprivation.
